newsitem.title: CANADA: Gandalf regains plant access, resumes ops.
newsitem.headline: Gandalf regains plant access, resumes ops.

text.p: Gandalf Technologies Inc said on Friday that it regained access to its plant in the Ottawa suburb of Nepean and resumed full operations after its landlord locked out about 300 workers on Thursday.
Early yesterday Glenview Corp shut the doors of Gandalf's rented headquarters but the computer equipment maker was given court permission to force its landlord to re-open the plant late in the day.
Also, Glenview was forced to pay Gandalf fixed legal costs, Gandalf said in a statement.

Glenview told local newspaper Ottawa Citizen that it was concerned Gandalf, which had been late with property taxes in the past, would not be able to ante up by a Friday deadline of 1700 EDT. The judge gave Gandalf until July 3 to pay.
"It's probably cost a fair bit of disruption to the company," said Marleau, Lemire Securities analyst Brian Piccioni.

Glenview could not have picked a worse time, the Citizen said. Gandalf traditionally makes up close to 70 percent of its revenues in the final month of each quarter and up to 20 percent in the last week.
"It's unlikely that they'll get financing -- it's a dead issue," said an analyst who declined to be identified.

Gandalf said on June 6 it had exceeded its available margin amount on its Royal Bank of Canada credit line. The line was chopped to C$13 million from C$20 million when Gandalf reported poor fiscal 1997 fourth quarter results in May and fell into technical default on its loan.
Shares in Gandalf, halted in the late morning while market players awaited the company's news today, dropped when they resumed trading.
Gandalf slipped another three cents to 0.90 on the Toronto Stock Exchange after falling 0.14 to 0.93 from Friday's open.
On Nasdaq shares fell 8/32 to 19/32 after the morning bell. "You don't want to have people investing in this stock," Piccioni added.
The anonymous analyst added that Gandalf had a better chance to find a buyer as the over-inflated share price tumbles, cutting the company's capital.
"Either the stock price erodes to such a point where a buyer steps in," he said. Or "they wither away."
Piccioni estimated that if Toronto shares slip to about 0.50, the company would be valued at about C$15-C$20 million. The price tag would increase to C$30-C$40 million once debt was tacked on.
Piccioni said the company will be under pressure with nervous creditors. "It would be likely that you see developments in the next few weeks."
Another anonymous analyst added that "Gandalf's options are dwindling by the week." He forecast that only the company's equipment would be bought out by Ottawa-based computer companies.
"I think it's a bad business and it's getting worse," he said.
